ONE BILL WILL NOT DEFINE THE ENTIRE MARKET.

The Crypto CLARITY Act remains one of the most important regulatory developments for the US digital asset industry.

The Senate Banking Committee advanced the legislation in May by a bipartisan 15–9 vote.

But the bill has not yet passed the full Senate and has not become law.

At the same time, the regulatory process is not standing still.

SEC Chair Paul Atkins has said that the Commission’s 2026 agenda includes:

• clearer rules for crypto capital formation
• bringing more digital asset products onshore
• custody guidance
• rules for trading tokenized securities onchain

This creates two parallel processes.

Congress can establish a permanent statutory framework and define agency authority.

Regulators can interpret existing laws and develop rules inside the authority they already have.

Those processes are connected.

They are not interchangeable.

Agency rulemaking cannot automatically replace legislation.

Legislation cannot implement itself without detailed regulatory work.

For digital asset companies, the important questions are therefore broader than:

“Will the CLARITY Act pass this week?”

They include:

• What rules are already changing?
• Which agency currently has authority?
• What requires new legislation?
• Which obligations will depend on future rulemaking?
• How long will implementation take after passage?

A headline can create momentum.

A functioning market structure requires:

- law

- rules

- implementation

- enforcement

Legislation defines the architecture.
Regulation turns it into an operating system.

A vulnerability in the Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol (BEEP) feature of Cisco IOS XE Software could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause a denial of service (DoS) condition on an affected device.
This vulnerability is due to improper handling when parsing a specific BEEP SOAP request. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a specific BEEP SOAP request to an affected device. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to cause the device to reload unexpectedly, resulting in a DoS condition.

Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address these vulnerabilities.
